title: API and Data Model Design Mindmap
summary: API design and data modeling are the two decisions that most constrain a system's evolvability and performance. A well-designed API is stable, predictable, and easy to consume. A well-designed data model serves the dominant access patterns efficiently and can evolve as the business changes. This lesson provides structured approaches to both: RESTful resource design, pagination patterns, data model choices, and the relationship between queries and schema.

sections.title: API Design Principles
paragraphs: A good API is a stable contract between a service and its consumers. It should be intuitive (consumers can guess endpoints and parameters from conventions), consistent (similar operations look similar across all endpoints), and evolvable (new functionality can be added without breaking existing consumers). REST achieves this through resource-oriented design: nouns in URLs, HTTP verbs for operations, standard status codes for outcomes. GraphQL achieves it through a schema that enables clients to request exactly the data they need.

Resource design in REST: use plural nouns for collections (/orders), nested resources for owned relationships (/users/{userId}/orders), and avoid verbs in URLs (not /createOrder, but POST /orders). HTTP verbs should be used semantically: GET for reads (idempotent, safe), POST for creates (not idempotent), PUT for full replacement (idempotent), PATCH for partial update (idempotent), DELETE for removal (idempotent). Using POST for everything works but loses the semantics that enable caching, retry safety, and browser/proxy behavior.

API versioning is a first-class concern. Breaking changes in an API break consumers—and consumers deploy on their own schedules. Versioning strategies: URL prefix (/v1/orders, /v2/orders)—most visible, easy to route; header versioning (Accept: application/vnd.api.v2+json)—cleaner URLs, harder to test; query parameter (?version=2)—simple but pollutes parameters. Additive changes (new optional fields, new endpoints) are non-breaking. Renaming fields, changing types, removing fields, and changing semantics are breaking changes requiring a new version.

Pagination is mandatory for any endpoint that returns a collection. Without it, a 'get all orders' endpoint returns millions of rows as the system grows, causing OOM errors and timeout failures. Options: offset-based pagination (?page=5&size=20)—simple, allows jumping to arbitrary pages, but inconsistent with concurrent inserts/deletes; cursor-based pagination (?after=cursor&limit=20)—consistent, efficient (uses index scan from cursor), but cannot jump to arbitrary pages. Cursor-based is the correct choice for most high-volume APIs; offset is acceptable for admin interfaces where jumping to page N is required.
bullets: Resource-oriented: plural nouns for collections; nested for ownership; verbs by HTTP method
Breaking vs. non-breaking changes: additive = non-breaking; rename/remove/type change = breaking
Versioning: URL prefix (/v1/) is most common; plan for it from the start
Cursor pagination: consistent, index-efficient; prefer over offset for high-volume APIs

sections.title: Data Model Design Patterns
paragraphs: Data model design starts with identifying entities, their attributes, and their relationships. Entity-Relationship modeling (ER diagrams) captures the logical model. The relational model normalizes this into tables with foreign keys—great for consistency and query flexibility. But the relational model must be adapted for each database's access patterns: what's normalized in PostgreSQL might be denormalized into a document in MongoDB or split across multiple tables in Cassandra.

One-to-many relationships: a user has many orders. In SQL: foreign key (order.user_id references users.id). In NoSQL document store: embed orders array in the user document (good if orders are always accessed with the user) or separate collections with a reference (good if orders are queried independently). The embedding vs. referencing decision in document databases is driven by the query pattern: if you always load orders when loading a user, embed; if you sometimes load orders without loading the user, reference.

Many-to-many relationships: users follow users, products have multiple categories. In SQL: a junction table (user_follows: follower_id, followee_id). In NoSQL: embed the relationship list in one side (user.following_ids array) for small cardinality, or use a separate entity for high-cardinality many-to-many (a 50M-follower celebrity can't embed 50M IDs in their user document). In Cassandra, model each direction of the relationship as a separate table—a table for 'users I follow' and a table for 'users who follow me'.

Temporal data modeling captures how entities change over time. Slowly changing dimension (SCD) patterns from data warehousing address this: Type 1 (overwrite—no history), Type 2 (new row per version—full history with valid_from/valid_to timestamps), Type 3 (add columns for current and previous value—limited history). For event sourcing, the event log itself is the temporal model. For analytics, Type 2 enables point-in-time queries ('what was this customer's status on 2024-01-15?').
bullets: Embed vs. reference in document DB: driven by co-access pattern—always together = embed
Many-to-many in Cassandra: model both directions as separate tables
SCD Type 2: full temporal history with valid_from/valid_to; enables point-in-time queries
Query-first modeling: define access patterns first, then derive schema

sections.title: Database Schema for Common System Design Patterns
paragraphs: URL shortener schema: id (auto-increment or base62), long_url (varchar, indexed), short_code (varchar(8), unique indexed), created_at, user_id (nullable—anonymous vs. authenticated), clicks (counter, eventually consistent OK), expiry (nullable). The short_code is the lookup key—must be unique and fast to look up (unique index). Consider whether short codes are sequential (guessable) or random (requires generation strategy). Rate limiting: per user_id if authenticated, per IP if anonymous.

Social feed schema (relational): users (id, username, created_at), posts (id, user_id, content, created_at), follows (follower_id, followee_id), likes (user_id, post_id), comments (id, post_id, user_id, content). Key indexes: posts(user_id, created_at DESC) for user's posts, follows(follower_id) and follows(followee_id) for following/followers, likes(post_id) for like count. For scale: separate read and write paths, Redis cache for hot users' feeds, CDN for media.

Ride-hailing schema: trips (id, rider_id, driver_id, status, pickup_location, dropoff_location, start_time, end_time, fare), drivers (id, name, vehicle, current_location, status), ratings (trip_id, from_user_id, to_user_id, rating). The critical access pattern is geospatial: find available drivers within 5km of pickup. This requires a geospatial index (PostGIS, Redis GEOADD, or S2 cells). The trips table needs indexes on (rider_id, start_time) and (driver_id, start_time) for history queries and (status, pickup_location) for dispatcher queries.
bullets: URL shortener: short_code as unique primary key; redirect table optimized for point lookup
Social feed: posts indexed by (user_id, created_at); follows as separate table or adjacency list
Ride-hailing: geospatial index on driver location; trips indexed by rider, driver, and status
Design indexes for the dominant query patterns, not all possible queries

sections.title: API Error Handling and Idempotency
paragraphs: HTTP status codes should be used consistently and correctly. 200 OK for success, 201 Created for new resource creation (include Location header with new resource URL), 204 No Content for successful deletions, 400 Bad Request for client-side validation errors (include error details in response body), 401 Unauthorized for missing/invalid authentication, 403 Forbidden for valid authentication but insufficient permissions, 404 Not Found for missing resources, 409 Conflict for concurrent modification conflicts, 422 Unprocessable Entity for semantic errors (all fields valid but business rule violated), 429 Too Many Requests for rate limiting, 500 Internal Server Error for unhandled server errors, 503 Service Unavailable for circuit-open fallbacks.

Error response bodies should be structured and consistent: include an error code (machine-readable, stable identifier), a human-readable message, and optionally a details array for validation errors listing field-specific messages. The error code should be stable across API versions—consumers may switch on error codes in their error handling logic. The message is for developers, not end users (the client should translate to user-friendly copy in the UI).

Idempotency keys enable safe retries for non-idempotent POST requests. The client generates a unique UUID for each logical operation and includes it in the Idempotency-Key header. The server stores the idempotency key with the operation result for a configurable TTL (typically 24 hours). If the same idempotency key is received again, the server returns the original result without re-executing the operation. This is essential for payment APIs, order creation, and any state-modifying operation that may be retried due to network errors.
bullets: Status codes: 2xx success, 4xx client errors, 5xx server errors—use semantically correct codes
Structured error response: error_code (stable), message (human), details (field-level)
Idempotency-Key header: safe retry of POST operations; server deduplicates by key+TTL
Location header: 201 Created response includes URL of new resource

core.title: REST API Design
paragraphs: Resource-oriented URLs (plural nouns, nested for ownership), HTTP verbs by semantics, consistent error response structure, URL versioning (/v1/).
Cursor-based pagination for high-volume APIs; offset for small collections or admin interfaces.
Breaking change management: additive changes are safe; removals/renames/type changes require new version.
bullets: Idempotency-Key: safe retries for POST operations
Rate limiting: 429 with Retry-After header; communicate limit clearly
HATEOAS: include links in responses for discoverability (optional but recommended)

core.title: Data Model Design
paragraphs: Query-first: define access patterns before schema. Normalize for SQL; denormalize for NoSQL.
Embed vs. reference in document DB: co-access pattern decides. Many-to-many: junction table (SQL) or dual tables (Cassandra).
Index design: index for the dominant queries; avoid over-indexing (write amplification).
bullets: Foreign key placement: child table holds parent's ID
SCD Type 2: temporal history with valid_from/valid_to timestamps
Covering index: include frequently-read columns to enable index-only scans

deepDive.title: API Design for Scale and Evolution
paragraphs: GraphQL vs. REST trade-offs for scale: GraphQL enables clients to request exactly the data they need (eliminating over-fetching and under-fetching), supports type safety and introspection, and reduces API versioning needs through additive schema evolution. The costs: N+1 query problem (DataLoader solves this), caching complexity (REST caches at URL level; GraphQL POST requests are cache-unfriendly), arbitrary query depth and complexity attacks (use query depth limits and cost analysis), and steeper learning curve. GraphQL is the right choice for client-driven APIs with heterogeneous clients (mobile, web, 3rd-party) with different data needs.

Event-driven APIs (webhooks and event streams) complement synchronous REST. Webhooks push events to consumer-registered URLs: simple, widely supported, but unreliable (the consumer may be down when the event fires). Retry with exponential backoff and dead-letter queues address reliability. Event streams (Kafka, AWS EventBridge) provide durable, replayable delivery—the consumer can replay from any point. The architectural pattern: use REST for reads and synchronous mutations, webhooks or event streams for async notifications and cross-service integration.

API gateway pattern centralizes cross-cutting concerns: authentication/authorization (JWT validation before routing), rate limiting (per API key or user), request/response transformation, SSL termination, logging, and analytics. This keeps individual services free of infrastructure concerns. API gateways (AWS API Gateway, Kong, Apigee, custom Nginx) provide these features declaratively. The trade-off: an API gateway is an additional latency hop (5-20ms) and a potential SPOF (must be HA). Use it for public APIs; consider whether it adds value for internal service-to-service APIs.
bullets: GraphQL: eliminate over/under-fetching; type safety; needs DataLoader for N+1; cache complexity
Webhooks: push events; retry with backoff; dead-letter queue for undeliverable events
API gateway: centralize auth, rate limit, SSL; latency tradeoff; HA required
OpenAPI/Swagger: document REST APIs machine-readably; generate client SDKs and tests

expert.title: Schema Evolution and Backward Compatibility
paragraphs: Schema evolution in distributed systems is a first-class concern. Protobuf (Protocol Buffers) handles backward and forward compatibility through field numbering: existing fields must keep their numbers; new fields get new numbers; unknown fields are preserved. This allows producers and consumers to evolve their schemas independently as long as they follow the rules. Avro uses schema IDs embedded in messages; the schema registry stores all schemas; consumers look up the schema to deserialize. JSON Schema has weaker compatibility guarantees and relies on discipline rather than enforcement.

Database schema migrations in production: the expand-contract pattern (also called blue-green migration) enables zero-downtime schema changes. Expand: add new column/table alongside old (nullable or with default). Dual-write: write to both old and new schemas. Migrate: backfill existing data to new schema. Contract: once all code uses new schema and all data is migrated, remove old schema. This pattern allows rolling deploys to old and new code simultaneously without data inconsistency.

Semantic versioning for APIs: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. PATCH: bug fixes, no API change. MINOR: backward-compatible additions. MAJOR: breaking changes. The critical discipline: increment MAJOR version for any breaking change and maintain the previous version for a deprecation period (typically 6-12 months). Publish a deprecation timeline in API documentation and send deprecation headers (Sunset, Deprecation) in responses to inform consumers of upcoming breaking changes.

concepts: Resource-oriented design: plural nouns for collections, HTTP verbs for operations, nested URLs for ownership
Idempotency key: client-generated UUID for safe retries of non-idempotent POST operations
Cursor pagination: stable, index-efficient pagination using opaque cursor tokens
Offset pagination: simple page+size pagination; inconsistent with concurrent modifications
Embedding vs. referencing: document DB data modeling decision based on co-access patterns
Query-first schema design: define access patterns before defining schema
SCD Type 2: temporal history pattern with valid_from/valid_to timestamps
API versioning: URL prefix (/v1/), header, or query parameter; plan from day one
Breaking change: any change that causes existing consumers to fail without code changes
Expand-contract pattern: zero-downtime database schema migration strategy
GraphQL: schema-driven API; clients specify data requirements; eliminates over/under-fetching
API gateway: centralized cross-cutting concerns (auth, rate limiting, SSL, logging) for public APIs
practices: Design API versioning into the URL path from the first release (/v1/)—retrofitting versioning is painful
Use cursor-based pagination for any collection that grows with user activity
Implement idempotency keys for all state-modifying POST endpoints; store results for 24 hours
Design data schema with specific access patterns in mind—test with realistic queries before committing
Use the expand-contract pattern for all database schema changes in production
Return structured error responses with stable machine-readable error codes
Document breaking vs. non-breaking changes; maintain deprecated API versions for 6+ months
pitfalls: Using POST for all operations—loses idempotency semantics; makes retry and caching hard
No pagination on collection endpoints—unbounded results cause OOM errors at scale
Offset pagination for real-time feeds—inconsistent results when records are inserted/deleted during pagination
Breaking changes without versioning—existing consumers break silently with 500 errors
Embedding unlimited-size arrays in document DB—a user with 10M followers can't embed them in one document
Schema migration without expand-contract—adding NOT NULL column requires all code to write it simultaneously
Missing idempotency keys on payment APIs—retries on network failure cause double charges

examples.title: E-commerce Orders API Design
examples.description: A well-designed orders API: GET /v1/orders?after={cursor}&limit=20 (cursor pagination), POST /v1/orders (create order, returns 201 with Location: /v1/orders/ord_xyz), GET /v1/orders/{orderId} (get order), PATCH /v1/orders/{orderId} (partial update—status change only), DELETE /v1/orders/{orderId} (cancel order). Error response: {error_code: 'ORDER_NOT_FOUND', message: 'Order ord_xyz not found', request_id: 'req_abc'}. POST /v1/orders requires Idempotency-Key header; duplicates return the original response without re-charging.

examples.title: Social Network Schema
examples.description: A PostgreSQL schema for a social network: users (id UUID PK, username, email, created_at), posts (id UUID PK, user_id FK, content TEXT, created_at, media_urls TEXT[]). follows (follower_id FK, followee_id FK, created_at, PK(follower_id, followee_id)). likes (user_id FK, post_id FK, created_at, PK(user_id, post_id)). Key indexes: (user_id, created_at DESC) on posts for user timelines, (follower_id) and (followee_id) on follows for graph traversal. For scale, the follows table is sharded by follower_id; a separate inverted index (followees table) enables 'who follows this user' queries.

keyTakeaways: Resource-oriented REST APIs are predictable, cacheable, and evolvable—use HTTP verbs and status codes correctly
Cursor-based pagination is the correct default for high-volume APIs; offset pagination causes inconsistency at scale
Schema design should be query-driven: define the access patterns first, then design the schema to serve them
Idempotency keys transform dangerous POST retries into safe operations—essential for payment and order APIs
API versioning must be designed from day one; retrofitting versioning is expensive and disruptive
Expand-contract is the only way to do zero-downtime database schema migrations
GraphQL eliminates over/under-fetching at the cost of caching complexity and N+1 query risk
whyItMatters: API and data model design are the most consequential early decisions in a system. They determine what queries are possible, what integrations are feasible, how consumers evolve with the service, and whether the system can scale to meet growing demand. Getting them right early avoids painful migrations; getting them wrong creates years of technical debt.
reflectionQuestions: Design the API for a task management app (like Trello) with projects, boards, lists, and cards. Write out the top 5 endpoints with their HTTP methods, URLs, request/response schemas, and pagination strategy.
You need to migrate a user table to add a new required field (phone_number NOT NULL). How do you do this with zero downtime and without breaking existing services that don't yet write phone numbers?
Compare REST and GraphQL for a mobile app that has 10 different screens, each showing a different subset of user profile data. What are the trade-offs and which would you recommend?
A payment API endpoint that creates charges occasionally gets duplicate requests due to network retries. How do you design it to be safely retryable without double-charging?
numbersToKnow: Cursor pagination: typical page size 20-100 items; cursor is base64-encoded primary key or timestamp
Idempotency key TTL: 24 hours is industry standard (Stripe, Braintree)
API versioning support window: 6-12 months after deprecation announcement before removal
URL length limit: 2,048 characters (practical limit for GET parameters); use POST body for large filters
HTTP/2 max concurrent streams: 100 (default); multiplexes many API calls on one connection
GraphQL query depth limit: 10-15 levels; prevents N+1 attack via deeply nested queries

interviewQuestions: Design the data model and primary API endpoints for a URL shortening service. What indexes would you create and why?
What is cursor-based pagination and why is it preferred over offset pagination for social feed APIs?
Explain the expand-contract pattern for database schema migrations. Walk through migrating a nullable column to a NOT NULL column in production.
What is an idempotency key and how would you implement it on a payment API?
exercises: Design the full data model (ER diagram + schema + indexes) and REST API specification (top 10 endpoints with request/response schemas) for an Airbnb-like home rental platform.

Given an existing PostgreSQL orders table with 500M rows, design the migration plan to add a new required metadata column with a default value—with zero downtime, maintaining all existing indexes, and rolling out the change across 50 service instances that deploy independently.
Design a GraphQL schema for a news aggregator with articles, authors, and categories. Address the N+1 problem for fetching article authors, and implement cursor-based pagination for article lists.
